Thomas Helwys
tom'ūs hel'wis
n. (Thomas Helwys, c. 1575–c. 1616, English Baptist, founder of the first Baptist church on English soil and pioneer of religious liberty)
English Helwys, a Nottinghamshire surname; Thomas, from Aramaic Te'oma, a twin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thomas Helwys was a Nottinghamshire gentleman of Broxtowe Hall, trained at Gray's Inn, who funded and then shared the Amsterdam exile of John Smyth's congregation. When Smyth sought union with the Mennonites, Helwys refused, and about 1612 he led a dozen members back to England and gathered a church at Spitalfields outside London, the first Baptist congregation in the country. That year he published A Short Declaration of the Mistery of Iniquity, and sent a copy to King James with an inscription declaring that the king is a mortal man and has no authority over the immortal souls of his subjects. It is the first plea in English for liberty of conscience for all men, including, in his words, heretics, Turks and Jews. He was imprisoned in Newgate and died there within four years. Act 5:29 is the premise. Mat 22 renders to Caesar what is Caesar's, and the soul is not among those things. Rom 14 leaves each servant to stand or fall to his own master.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines conscience as internal or self-knowledge, and the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions; and liberty, as freedom from restraint.

expand to see more

CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; or the faculty, power or principle within us, which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions and affections.

LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense, and applicable to the body, or to the will or mind.

TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.

Key Scripture

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

1Pe 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Mat 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

2Co 5:20 — "Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God."

Modern Corruption

Helwys told King James that a mortal man has no jurisdiction over immortal souls, and died in Newgate for the sentence.

expand to see more

Helwys drew his argument from the nature of faith rather than from a theory of rights. A magistrate can compel attendance, silence a preacher, and fine a recusant; he cannot create belief, because belief is the soul's response to God and the soul is outside his commission. Mat 10:28 draws the same boundary from the other side, distinguishing what man can kill from what he cannot touch. 1Pe 3:15 commissions the believer to give an answer with meekness and fear, which assumes persuasion as the church's only proper instrument.

The modern misuse of Helwys is to enlist him for the claim that all religions are equally true or that the state must treat truth and error as indistinguishable. He believed nothing of the kind; he thought Rome and Islam damning errors and said so in the same book. His argument was that error is answered by preaching and not by prison. 2Co 5:20 gives the church its office, ambassadors who beseech, and an ambassador who reaches for the magistrate's sword has abandoned the embassy.

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — written to a king, from Newgate."

"“be ready always to give an answer” (1Pe 3:15) — persuasion, not compulsion."

"“we are ambassadors for Christ” (2Co 5:20) — the church's only office toward unbelievers."
